turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll pop the cuff on before the doctor calls you. You look a bit washed out, hey.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. I feel like a wet rag, and I've been stuck in that passage forever. Load shedding, the robot was a mess. I'm not in the mood.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Shame. Blood pressure is one twenty eight over seventy eight. Pulse is seventy six. Oxygen sat is ninety eight percent. Doctor will be in now now.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Howzit. I'm doctor Naidoo. What's brought you in today, in your own words?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): The driving. I want to know if I can get back behind the wheel. Two years with no fits and I'm still on taxis. It's ridiculous.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): There's also last month, doc. He won't bring it up.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll get there. First, the epilepsy. What tablets are you actually on?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Levetirasetam. Five hundred milligrams, morning and night, for the epilepsy. I've had it about twelve years. The chemist label says Keppra half the time.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the fits themselves. When was the last proper one?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Two years back. I haven't had a proper fit since we changed the tablets.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): What did you come off?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The Epilim. I stopped it in March, when we switched. I never took the lamotrogine they mentioned at the hospital. They didn't actually give it to me.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been taking the levetiracetam every single day?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly, ja. Down at the coast last month the packet was in the other bag. I missed some mornings. Two, maybe three, err, I don't actually know.
[SEG0015] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It felt like more days than that. I wasn't counting the tablets, mind.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. Who's come with you today?

[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm his sister, I stay over a few nights a week and help with the meds on those long shifts. Last month at my flat he went blank, stared at the wall maybe a minute, didn't answer when I called him. Then he just carried on.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): That is not a fit. I did not blank out. I was thinking about work. You're blowing it up because you worry.

[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to call that a seizure sitting here. It might have been a little absence, or you might just have zoned out because you're flat and exhausted. I won't land on either one today. A level will help the picture, but the number on its own doesn't decide it.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't actually know. Wonderful.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): How has the rest of you been, day to day?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I've overdone it, honestly, I feel like a wet rag most afternoons. My feet feel dead when I climb off a long shift, like they're somebody else's. There's a frog in my throat in the mornings as well, which irritates me. At the warehouse I can't hear myself think with the forklifts, but that's just the noise, not my ears.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did that dead feeling in the feet start?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. I can't say. A while back. I really don't know the date.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any shaking fits, any wetting yourself, any biting of the tongue?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Not in the two years, and not last month.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Headaches? Trouble with the eyes?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. Eyes are fine.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your breathing, your chest, your stomach. Anything playing up in those systems?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine. Stomach's fine.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): On the family side, epilepsy, sugar, pressure, any of that?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, my father had diabetes in his fifties, my mother did not, my older brother had epilepsy as a child but he grew out of it, and my other sister has pressure but no sugar.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about the days themselves. Work, food, exercise, drink?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I pack stock at a warehouse in Germiston, twelve hour shifts, four on and three off. Food is whatever the canteen dishes up, mostly pap and stew, a kota if I'm late. I don't exercise, not since the fits, and it's a beer or two on a Friday after shift, nothing through the week. I don't smoke.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll have a quick look at the feet. Pulses are present both sides. Light touch is a bit dull on both soles. I don't find any weakness.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Can we do the licence part. That's why I came. I'm fed up with this.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): With that possible blank spell still on the table, I can't support you driving today. If those two clear years hold and this wasn't a seizure, we talk about the private licence at the review, not this morning. Please don't drive until we've reviewed it. And don't skip the levetiracetam when you travel, even a morning or two matters.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Fine. I heard you.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll book a levetiracetam blood level, because of the missed tablets and that spell, and a full blood count while we're there. Come back in two weeks and we'll go through the results and the driving again. Try to rest a bit if the shifts allow, hey.
[SEG0040] person_1 (NURSE): I can slot those bloods for Thursday morning, before you take the tablet, so it's a trough level. Lab is downstairs.

spec.situation: Adult with epilepsy on levetiracetam, seizure-free for two years, asks about driving; missed doses when travelling; relative saw a 'blank spell' last month; doctor reviews and plans a blood test.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
